title: Hypertension & Hypertensive Crisis: Accurate Measurement, Organ Protection and Safe Reduction
html:
Hypertension is usually silent, but its cumulative vascular stress can injure the brain, heart, kidneys, eyes, and arteries. A very high number becomes an emergency when it is accompanied by new or worsening target-organ damage. The RN must first verify measurement quality, then rapidly distinguish chronic or severe asymptomatic hypertension from a hypertensive emergency—without dismissing danger or lowering pressure so quickly that organ perfusion falls.

Learning goals

  • Obtain and validate blood-pressure measurements using correct preparation, positioning, cuff size, and technique.
  • Classify adult blood pressure in context and recognize white-coat, masked, resistant, and secondary patterns.
  • Distinguish severe hypertension from hypertensive emergency by evidence of acute target-organ injury.
  • Prioritize nursing care for neurologic, cardiac, aortic, renal, ophthalmic, and pregnancy-related emergencies.
  • Monitor oral and IV antihypertensive therapy for response, hypotension, electrolyte change, and organ hypoperfusion.
  • Teach accurate home monitoring, medication safety, lifestyle measures, and individualized escalation thresholds.

Accuracy comes before classification

Blood pressure changes with pain, anxiety, activity, talking, nicotine, caffeine, temperature, bladder fullness, medications, positioning, cuff size, and technique. Unless immediate instability requires simultaneous action, allow quiet rest, use a validated device and correctly sized cuff on a bare supported arm at heart level, support the back, keep feet flat and legs uncrossed, and avoid conversation. Repeat unexpected values and compare both arms initially when appropriate.

A cuff that is too small can produce a falsely high result; an unsupported arm, dangling legs, or active conversation can also distort the reading. In atrial fibrillation, tremor, severe vascular disease, or weak perfusion, automated devices may be unreliable. Verify manually or with an appropriate alternative while assessing the client. Never delay emergency treatment merely to obtain a cosmetically perfect number.

Validate the number—then assess the person
A repeat pressure is not a substitute for evaluating chest pain, dyspnea, neurologic change, severe back pain, pregnancy symptoms, or poor perfusion.

Know the adult categories, but diagnose from patterns

Under the 2025 ACC/AHA adult guideline, normal blood pressure is below 120/80 mm Hg; elevated pressure is systolic 120–129 with diastolic below 80; stage 1 hypertension is systolic 130–139 or diastolic 80–89; and stage 2 is systolic at least 140 or diastolic at least 90. When systolic and diastolic values fall into different categories, use the higher category.

A diagnosis generally requires appropriate readings on separate occasions and may be confirmed with home or ambulatory monitoring. White-coat hypertension is elevated in the clinical setting but not outside it. Masked hypertension appears acceptable in the clinic but elevated outside it. Both require validated measurement and follow-up; neither can be diagnosed from a single casual reading.

Connect chronic pressure with target-organ risk

Persistent hypertension promotes endothelial injury, arterial stiffness, atherosclerosis, left-ventricular hypertrophy, impaired ventricular filling, kidney damage, retinopathy, and small- and large-vessel brain disease. Risk is influenced by the level and duration of pressure plus age, smoking, lipids, diabetes, kidney disease, existing cardiovascular disease, pregnancy status, social conditions, and treatment access.

Assess for prior stroke or transient ischemic attack, coronary disease, heart failure, peripheral arterial disease, aortic disease, kidney disease, retinopathy, diabetes, sleep apnea, pregnancy complications, and family history. Review medications, over-the-counter products, supplements, alcohol, stimulants, nicotine, cocaine or methamphetamine exposure, sodium intake, activity, sleep, and adherence barriers without blame.

Severe hypertension is not automatically an emergency

In a nonpregnant adult, pressure above 180 systolic and/or 120 diastolic is severe. If the reading is unexpected and the client is stable, repeat it correctly and immediately assess for symptoms and acute organ injury. Severe pressure without new target-organ damage usually needs prompt clinician contact, medication review, and close follow-up rather than reflex IV treatment or hospitalization.

A hypertensive emergency is severe pressure with acute or worsening target-organ damage. The diagnosis depends on the organ threat, not a number alone. Examples include hypertensive encephalopathy, intracranial hemorrhage or selected acute ischemic stroke situations, acute coronary syndrome, acute pulmonary edema, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury, retinal hemorrhage or papilledema, and severe pregnancy-related hypertension with preeclampsia or eclampsia.

Search for acute target-organ injury

Perform a rapid ABC and perfusion assessment. Ask about severe or new headache, confusion, seizure, weakness, numbness, speech or vision change, loss of consciousness, chest pressure, tearing chest or back pain, dyspnea, orthopnea, pregnancy or postpartum status, reduced urine output, and recent medication or substance exposure.

Assess mental status, pupils, speech, facial symmetry, strength and sensation, gait when safe, lung sounds, oxygenation, heart rate and rhythm, pulses in all extremities as indicated, skin perfusion, edema, jugular veins, urine output, and visual complaints. Compare arm pressures when aortic dissection is suspected if this does not delay emergency imaging and treatment.

Anticipate ECG, troponin, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, urinalysis, pregnancy testing when relevant, chest imaging, brain imaging, aortic imaging, and funduscopic evaluation based on presentation. Normal results in one organ do not clear the others.

Hypertensive emergency requires controlled IV treatment

Activate emergency or critical-care support, establish continuous pressure and cardiac monitoring, obtain IV access, and treat the specific organ syndrome. Titrated IV medication is chosen according to the affected organ, comorbidities, pregnancy status, heart rate, kidney and liver function, and contraindications. An arterial catheter may be used for continuous measurement in selected unstable clients.

For many hypertensive emergencies, pressure is lowered in a controlled, stepwise manner rather than normalized immediately. Chronic hypertension shifts autoregulation, so an abrupt large reduction can cause cerebral, coronary, or renal ischemia. Exact targets and timing differ for aortic dissection, acute ischemic stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, ACS, pulmonary edema, and pregnancy emergencies. Follow the syndrome-specific protocol and qualified orders.

The goal is organ protection, not a normal number
Report neurologic decline, chest pain, worsening dyspnea, cool skin, oliguria, or a sudden pressure drop during treatment. These may signal inadequate perfusion even if the displayed pressure looks “better.”

Specific emergencies require different priorities

Aortic dissection: Sudden severe chest or back pain, pulse or pressure differences, new neurologic findings, or aortic regurgitation signs require immediate imaging and a rapid heart-rate and pressure-control pathway. Reduce shear with protocol-directed beta blockade before adding selected vasodilators unless contraindicated; vasodilation alone can provoke reflex tachycardia.

Acute pulmonary edema: Sit the client upright when tolerated, support oxygenation and ventilation, and prepare syndrome-appropriate vasodilator and diuretic therapy when hemodynamics permit. A routine fluid bolus can worsen congestion.

Neurologic emergency: Protect airway and seizure safety, document a focused neurologic baseline, determine last-known well for possible stroke, and avoid applying a generic pressure target. Cerebral perfusion and eligibility for reperfusion or hemorrhage management shape the goal.

Pregnancy or postpartum emergency: Severe hypertension with headache, vision change, right-upper-quadrant or epigastric pain, dyspnea, hyperreflexia, seizure, or laboratory abnormalities may represent preeclampsia/eclampsia. Activate obstetric emergency protocols. Antihypertensive and magnesium therapy require maternal respiratory, reflex, urine, fetal, and medication-toxicity monitoring as appropriate.

Oral therapy is for chronic control, not rapid rescue

First-line chronic therapy commonly includes thiazide-type diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and calcium-channel blockers, selected according to comorbidities, pregnancy potential, kidney function, electrolytes, age, interactions, cost, and client preference. Stage 2 hypertension may require two complementary medications. Beta blockers have specific indications but are not the universal first choice for uncomplicated hypertension.

Monitor thiazide-type therapy for sodium, potassium, uric acid, glucose, volume depletion, and kidney effects. ACE inhibitors and ARBs can increase potassium and creatinine and are contraindicated in pregnancy; do not combine them routinely. Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers can cause edema, flushing, or headache. Beta blockers can cause bradycardia and may mask adrenergic signs of hypoglycemia. Teach clients not to stop clonidine or beta blockers abruptly because rebound or ischemic harm can occur.

Resistant hypertension demands verification

Before labeling pressure resistant, verify technique, cuff fit, adherence and access, medication doses and combinations, white-coat effect, and substances that raise pressure. NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants, some contraceptive or hormone therapies, corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, licorice, excess alcohol, and illicit stimulants can contribute.

Secondary causes include kidney parenchymal disease, renal artery disease, primary aldosteronism, obstructive sleep apnea, thyroid or parathyroid disease, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, coarctation, and medication or substance effects. Clues include abrupt onset, very young age, sudden loss of prior control, disproportionate organ injury, hypokalemia, episodic symptoms, abdominal bruit, or resistant pressure. The RN gathers the pattern and supports ordered evaluation rather than assigning the cause.

Orthostatic safety is part of blood-pressure care

Older adults, clients with autonomic dysfunction, volume depletion, diabetes, Parkinson disease, or multiple antihypertensives may develop orthostatic symptoms. Measure lying and standing pressures and pulse according to protocol when indicated, protect against falls, and ask about dizziness, near-syncope, meals, toileting, and medication timing. A good seated value is not successful treatment if the client falls when standing.

When titrating therapy, evaluate both hypertension control and tolerability: mentation, activity, perfusion, kidney function, electrolytes, edema, pulse, orthostatic symptoms, and adherence. Individual goals may differ for frailty, limited life expectancy, pregnancy, autonomic disease, or competing illness.

Lifestyle treatment is active treatment

Support a heart-healthy eating pattern, sodium reduction appropriate to the client, potassium-rich foods when kidney function and medications make them safe, regular physical activity, weight management, tobacco cessation, alcohol moderation, and adequate sleep. Screen for sleep apnea and address stress and social barriers. Avoid moralizing: food access, housing, work schedules, cost, language, and safe places to exercise affect the plan.

Medication and lifestyle treatment work together. Do not imply that a client caused hypertension or can always replace indicated medication through behavior alone.

Teach accurate home monitoring

Recommend a validated upper-arm device with the correct cuff size. Have the client avoid exercise, smoking, and caffeine shortly before measurement; empty the bladder; rest quietly; sit with back supported, feet flat, legs uncrossed, and bare arm supported at heart level; avoid talking; and take readings at the times and frequency in the care plan. Ask the client to bring the device and log for comparison.

Teach how to respond to a severe home reading: remain still, repeat after at least one minute using correct technique, assess for new concerning symptoms, and follow the written plan. A repeated pressure above 180/120 with chest pain, dyspnea, back pain, weakness, numbness, vision change, difficulty speaking, or another acute symptom requires emergency services. A similarly severe reading without symptoms still warrants prompt professional contact rather than self-adjusting medication.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Obtain a valid pressure, symptoms, neurologic and cardiopulmonary findings, perfusion, urine, pregnancy status, medication and substance history, prior values, comorbidities, and adherence barriers.
  2. Analyze cues: Separate measurement error and chronic elevation from severe asymptomatic hypertension and acute target-organ injury; identify the organ syndrome driving urgency.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Aortic dissection, stroke or hemorrhage, encephalopathy, ACS, pulmonary edema, eclampsia, and acute kidney injury require immediate action.
  4. Generate solutions: Activate syndrome-specific support, plan controlled pressure reduction, obtain targeted diagnostics, protect perfusion, and correct contributing causes.
  5. Take action: Monitor continuously, administer titrated therapy through the authorized pathway, institute seizure, fall, or respiratory precautions, and avoid abrupt nonspecific lowering.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess pressure trend, neurologic status, chest or back pain, breathing, oxygenation, pulses, perfusion, urine, kidney function, electrolytes, adverse effects, and teach-back.

Clinical example

A client has a repeated pressure of 224/128 mm Hg, sudden tearing back pain, unequal radial pulses, and new leg weakness. The RN does not give an unscheduled oral medication and wait. The RN activates emergency support, maintains bed rest, obtains continuous monitoring and IV access, reports the suspected aortic emergency, and prepares rapid imaging and protocol-directed heart-rate and pressure control. Neurologic status, pulses, pain, pressure, and perfusion are reassessed continuously because the goal is to reduce aortic shear while preserving organ blood flow.

Original educational synthesis. Blood-pressure diagnosis, treatment thresholds and goals, drug selection and dosing, emergency reduction targets, stroke and aortic pathways, and pregnancy care require current clinical data, validated equipment, authorized orders, local protocols, specialist input, and qualified supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, or an official ACC, AHA, or NCSBN product.
